clips.text_en_b2: Forced to pick a single asset to hold over the next decade, would you go with Bitcoin or gold? The /biz/ thread is split right down the middle. Gold bugs hammer home the point that it carries five millennia of monetary history, whereas Bitcoiners counter that it is inherently scarce, borderless, and primed to become the next global reserve asset. Neither camp is willing to concede ground.
clips.text_en_c1: Should one be compelled to allocate capital to a single asset for the coming decade, the perennial debate between Bitcoin and gold resurfaces with renewed vigour on /biz/. Gold advocates invoke its five-millennium track record as a monetary store of value, whilst Bitcoin maximalists counter that its digital scarcity and decentralised architecture position it as the contemporary reserve asset. The thread remains evenly divided, with neither camp gaining the upper hand. For those simultaneously juggling open futures positions, contemplating such macro quandaries feels less like prudent diversification and more like a futile exercise in futility, prompting an exasperated chuckle rather than genuine conviction.
clips.text_en_c2: A thread on /biz/ has reignited a perennial parlour game: if constrained to a single asset for the coming decade, would one elect Bitcoin or physical gold? The fissure is, as ever, total. Gold partisans invoke five millennia of monetary precedent, central-bank accumulation, and the metal's enduring role as a crisis hedge. Their digital-native counterparts counter that programmability, verifiable scarcity, and an accelerating institutional embrace position Bitcoin as the nascent reserve asset of a de-dollared financial order. Neither camp persuades the other, since the underlying ontological dispute — whether money is fundamentally a store of narrative or of arithmetic — admits no empirical resolution.

clips.text_zh: OpenAI 又嚟⋯⋯兩個 mathematician 用 claude + gpt 做緊嘅問題，OpenAI 直接出 paper 話自己 swarm agent 解咗，credit 都冇俾人。AI 連數學家都搶，仲有咩係安全 🧐
clips.text_en_b1: Two mathematicians, Alpöge and Buckmaster, were collaborating on a problem using Claude and GPT and made real progress. Then OpenAI published a paper claiming their agent swarm solved the same problem on its own. The approach was very similar. The mathematicians were not credited.
clips.source_hint: /g/ thread on OpenAI allegedly stealing a math result

signal.rationale: AI ethics story, not a trade setup

clips.text_en_b2: Two mathematicians, Alpöge and Buckmaster, had been quietly collaborating on a research problem using Claude and GPT and were making tangible headway. Then OpenAI dropped a paper claiming their own agent swarm had independently cracked the same problem — using a strikingly similar approach, yet failing to credit the original duo. If AI outfits are now muscling in on mathematicians, one has to wonder what niche is actually safe anymore.
clips.text_en_c1: Two mathematicians, Alpöge and Buckmaster, had been making substantive progress on a problem through iterative collaboration with Claude and GPT. Shortly thereafter, OpenAI released a paper asserting that their agent swarm had independently arrived at a comparable solution. The methodological overlap was striking, yet no acknowledgement of the prior work was forthcoming. Should established AI laboratories feel entitled to appropriate intellectual contributions from individual researchers without attribution, the implications for academic integrity are profoundly disquieting. If even mathematics, long regarded as a bastion of rigorous attribution, cannot withstand such incursions, the question of which domains remain secure becomes increasingly rhetorical.
clips.text_en_c2: Two mathematicians, Alpöge and Buckmaster, had been making substantive headway on an open problem by orchestrated deployment of Claude and GPT as collaborative research assistants. OpenAI then published a paper whose central claim — that their proprietary agent swarm had independently resolved the same question — sits uncomfortably adjacent to the prior work, both in methodology and in substance. No acknowledgement was extended to the original contributors. The episode, whatever its technical merits, crystallises a gathering anxiety: that the very laboratories tasked with augmenting human cognition are increasingly inclined to appropriate it, with attribution reduced to a discretionary courtesy rather than an institutional norm.

clips.text_en_b2: Another /pol/ thread has devolved into the familiar whites-versus-Indians culture war, claiming Westerners only romanticised India back when it stayed subservient and spiritually accessible to hippie tourists. Now that India wields genuine global clout, the poster argues, those same attitudes have curdled into outright hostility. The whole debate feels completely divorced from anything resembling real life — let alone anyone's actual surveying job.
clips.text_en_c1: A characteristic /pol/ thread has devolved into familiar racial sparring, this time concerning Western attitudes toward India. The prevailing argument, distilled, suggests that European populations historically celebrated non-Western cultures only insofar as those cultures remained deferential. India was once romanticised as a destination where disenchanted Westerners might pursue spiritual enlightenment. Now that the nation wields genuine geopolitical influence, the poster contends, that affection has curdled into open antagonism. For the average reader, whose professional obligations, such as a surveying assignment, bear no relation whatsoever to these abstruse cultural grievances, the spectacle amounts to little more than performative outrage divorced from tangible consequence.
clips.text_en_c2: The latest /pol/ provocation rehearses a familiar thesis: Western affection for ostensibly exotic cultures tends to flourish precisely so long as those cultures remain deferential. India, in this framing, was long cherished as a spiritual reservoir — a locale where disaffected Western seekers could transact in mysticism on terms entirely of their own devising. Yet as New Delhi has accrued genuine geopolitical weight, the register of commentary has palpably soured, transitioning from reverent curiosity to something more openly resentful. Whether this constitutes a coherent ideological position or merely the predictable reflux of displaced influence remains, charitably, open to interpretation.

clips.text_zh: /fit/ 有人問 calories in calories out 係咪低 IQ。我都想知⋯⋯我日日做 surveying 行到死死，點解 body composition 仲係咁樣。肥仔信叫我聽日夾去 gym，唔知會唔會去 🧐
clips.text_en_b1: The poster argues that calories in, calories out is a useless tautology. Knowing you stored the calories does not explain why you stored them. It is like answering 'why is Elon Musk rich' with 'he took in more money than he spent' — true, but it tells you nothing.
clips.text_en_b2: The /fit/ thread takes aim at the calories-in-calories-out crowd, calling it a useless tautology dressed up as science. Sure, knowing the calories were stored explains what happened, but it completely sidesteps why the body held onto them in the first place. The poster likens it to answering 'why is Elon Musk rich' with 'because he earned more than he spent' — technically accurate, yet utterly devoid of insight.
clips.text_en_c1: A poster on /fit/ contends that the calories-in-calories-out framework constitutes a vacuous oversimplification masquerading as nutritional science. Identifying that one has consumed surplus energy merely establishes that excess intake occurred, not the underlying hormonal, metabolic, or behavioural mechanisms that precipitated it. The analogy offered is apt: asserting that Elon Musk is wealthy because his revenues exceeded his expenditures is technically accurate yet explanatorily vacuous. For those whose physically demanding occupations yield negligible aesthetic returns despite meticulous caloric accounting, such critiques resonate uncomfortably. Whether this epiphany will translate into actually attending tomorrow's proposed gym session with fellow trainees remains, however, decidedly uncertain.
clips.text_en_c2: A /fit/ regular has taken up cudgels against the Calories In, Calories Out orthodoxy, contending that the framework is less a mechanistic explanation than a semantic tautology — observing that stored energy exists does not illuminate the hormonal, neurological, and behavioural pathways through which it came to be stored. The analogy deployed is illustrative: to say Musk is affluent because revenue exceeded expenditure is technically defensible yet explanatorily vacuous. For those whose professions involve considerable ambulation yet whose physiques remain stubbornly refractory to intervention, the post resonates as a clinical rejoinder to received nutritional wisdom.

clips.text_en_c2: Tite Kubo's recently unveiled one-shot, BLEACH THE HIGH SCHOOL WARFARE, vanished from Japanese retail within twenty-four hours, with aftermarket premiums already commanding multiples of cover price. Industry whispers suggest the publisher is angling for a monthly short-form serialisation, alongside an anime adaptation, a feature film, and a live-action production. The spectacle of singular creative bandwidth is, for the struggling aspirant, equal parts inspiring and galling.
